Tourism Industry in the Democratic Republic of the Congo Faces Crisis as Regional Bloc Imposes Sanctions

Tourism firms in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) are facing an abrupt and severe crisis following the announcement by the East African Community (EAC) of targeted sanctions on Congolese tourism enterprises, including the suspension of collaboration on cross-border tour packages and the freezing of joint marketing initiatives. The move, announced on Tuesday, comes amid escalating diplomatic tensions between the DRC and several EAC member states, and has already sent shockwaves across the country's tourism sector.

Under the new measures, EAC member states have suspended all bilateral tourism agreements with the DRC, blocked access to shared regional tourism sites, and prohibited EAC-based travel agencies from selling packages to Congolese destinations. Several key attractions operated by Congolese tourism firms, notably in the Virunga and Garamba regions, have been affected, with cross-border guided tours halted and joint conservation-tourism projects put on indefinite hold.

The impact on Congolese tourism operators has been immediate. Speaking to the Congolese Tourism Association, its president, Emmanuel Kabila, described the situation as “an existential threat for our sector.” He added, “More than 60% of our annual bookings rely on regional partnerships and joint initiatives. With these suspended, companies across the country are experiencing mass cancellations.”

Firms such as Safari Kivu and Congo Adventure Expeditions reported up to 85% of their foreign group tours for the coming quarter have already been cancelled, with further losses expected if the situation persists. “Our guides, rangers, and office staff are in limbo,” said Christine Mbayo, director of Safari Kivu. “We have no clarity on when or if we can resume normal operations.”

A survey by the National Union of Tourism Workers estimated that over 7,000 workers in the sector are facing immediate furlough or termination, with many more at risk if the impasse continues. “We are urging the government to find a diplomatic solution,” said union representative Pascal Ilunga. “Our members depend on the flow of regional tourists to support their families.”

Local analysts warn that the longer the blockade on regional tourism cooperation lasts, the more difficult it will be for Congolese firms to retain skilled staff and maintain their sites. “Tourism is uniquely vulnerable to these kinds of geopolitical shocks,” commented analyst Laura Mbuyi. “Recovery may take years, especially for remote and conservation-focused operators.”

As of press time, negotiations between the DRC and EAC are ongoing, but no breakthrough has been reported. The Congolese tourism sector remains on high alert as the crisis unfolds.
